lead: A screw jack lifts a heavy load with a small effort by turning an inclined plane that has been wrapped around a cylinder. That is all a screw thread is. Friction on the thread, measured by the friction angle φ, decides how much torque you must apply, how much mechanical advantage you get, how efficient the jack is, and whether the load stays up when you let go. Screw jacks raise cars in garages and level heavy machinery on shop floors, and the same thread analysis sizes the lead screw of a lathe.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.4 for the friction angle φ = tan⁻¹ μ, and moments about a point from Unit 2, Statics of Rigid Bodies.

sections.h3: Lead, mean radius and lead angle

blocks.text: A screw thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder. One full turn of the screw moves the nut a distance L along the axis; L is the lead. The pitch is the gap between neighbouring thread crests. On a single-start thread the lead equals the pitch; on a double-start thread the lead is twice the pitch. The formulas need the lead, so read the question for the number of starts.
Unroll one turn of the thread at the mean radius r and you get a right triangle. The base is 2πr, the length of one turn. The height is the lead L. The angle of this ramp is the lead angle α.

blocks.where: L is the lead (mm), r is the mean radius (mm) where the thread carries load, and α is the lead angle (use the same angle mode on your calculator throughout).

blocks.text: The mean radius is roughly halfway between the outside radius and the core radius of the screw. Use radius everywhere. Putting the diameter d in place of r doubles the torque, and halves tan α, so the lead angle comes out roughly half its true value.

items: Find the lead L = pitch × number of starts (in mm), then convert it to metres.
Write the mean radius in metres: r.
Compute tan α = L/(2πr), then α.
Compute the friction angle φ = tan⁻¹ μ from Chapter 3.4.
Get the torque from T = W r tan(α + φ), then the effort from P = T/R.

blocks.text: The thread is a rough incline, so this is the block-on-incline idea of Chapter 3.5 bent into a circle, close to the wedge of Chapter 3.6. While the load rises, friction on the thread opposes the motion, so the reaction from the thread is tilted by φ from the normal, against the turning direction. Resolving along and across the incline gives a driving force W tan(α + φ) at the mean radius.

blocks.where: T is the torque on the screw (N·m), W is the load (N), r is the mean radius (m), α is the lead angle and φ = tan⁻¹ μ is the friction angle.
P is the effort at the handle (N) and R is the handle radius (m). The handle is a lever, so a long handle turns a large torque with a small push.

blocks.text: Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort: W/P = R/(r tan(α + φ)). It is a pure number with no units. Raising the load by one lead takes one full turn, so the useful work is W L and the work you supply is P × 2πR.
η = W L / (P × 2πR) = tan α / tan(α + φ)
blocks.where: η is the efficiency, a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

blocks.text: The two forms agree because L = 2πr tan α and P × 2πR = 2πrW tan(α + φ). Real jacks run at about 15% to 40% efficiency, which is why a car jack needs many turns for a short lift. The lost work heats the thread.

Release the handle with the load still up. The load now tries to screw the jack down, so friction reverses and helps you. The load can turn the screw by itself only if α is bigger than φ. The condition for a self-locking jack is therefore φ ≥ α, that is μ ≥ tan α.

Self-locking has a price. At the boundary φ = α the efficiency is tan α / tan 2α = (1 − tan²α)/2, a little under 0.5. So no self-locking jack can be better than about 50% efficient, and most are far worse. That is a fair trade: a jack that unwinds under a car is a disaster.

Two refinements are left out here. A V-thread groove raises the effective friction to about μ/cos β, where β is the half angle of the thread. A collar under the load adds its own friction torque. Both belong to a machine-design course.

figure.caption: From lead and mean radius to the lead angle, then friction angle, torque, effort and the self-locking check. The lead angle of 1.82° is far below the friction angle of 8.53°, which is why the jack holds the load by itself.

spec.title: Screw jack
spec.aria: A screw jack calculation flow with lead 5 mm, mean radius 25 mm, lead angle 1.82 degrees, friction angle 8.53 degrees, torque 45.7 N m, effort 152 N, and the self-locking check.

examples.question: A screw jack has mean radius r = 25 mm and lead L = 5 mm (single start). The coefficient of friction between screw and nut is μ = 0.15. A load W = 10 kN is to be raised. Find (a) the torque needed on the screw, (b) the effort at the end of a handle of radius R = 300 mm, (c) the efficiency, and (d) state whether the jack is self-locking.
steps: Convert to metres and newtons: r = 0.025 m, L = 0.005 m, R = 0.3 m, W = 10 000 N.
Efficiency η = tan α / tan(α + φ) = 0.03183/0.1827 = 0.174, that is 17.4%.
Compare angles: φ = 8.53° is greater than α = 1.82°, so the jack is self-locking.
examples.answer: T = 45.7 N·m, P ≈ 152 N, η ≈ 17.4%, and since φ = 8.53° > α = 1.82° the jack is self-locking.
examples.check:
import math
W = 10000.0
r = 0.025
L = 0.005
mu = 0.15
R = 0.3
alpha = math.atan(L/(2*math.pi*r))
phi = math.atan(mu)
T = W*r*math.tan(alpha+phi)
P = T/R
eta = math.tan(alpha)/math.tan(alpha+phi)
print(round(T,1))
print(round(P,0))
print(round(eta,3))
print(round(math.degrees(alpha),2))
print(round(math.degrees(phi),2))

traps: Pitch for lead: a double-start thread with 3 mm pitch has L = 6 mm. Using 3 mm halves tan α and roughly halves the lead angle, and it lowers the torque by only a few per cent because φ dominates α + φ.
Diameter for radius in both L/(2πr) and W r tan(α + φ).
Stopping at the torque when the question asks for the effort; divide the torque by the handle radius R.
Calling a jack self-locking because μ looks large; you must compare φ with α, not μ with 1.
Calculator in the wrong angle mode, or writing η = tan(α + φ)/tan α and reporting an efficiency above 100%.

quiz.q: Define lead and pitch of a screw thread and give the relation between them for a single-start thread.
quiz.a: Lead L is the axial distance the nut moves in one full turn. Pitch is the distance between neighbouring crests. For a single-start thread L equals the pitch; for an n-start thread L = n × pitch.

quiz.q: State the condition for a screw jack to be self-locking.
quiz.a: φ ≥ α, that is tan φ ≥ tan α or μ ≥ L/(2πr). Friction alone then holds the load when the effort is removed.

quiz.q: Why is the efficiency of a screw jack below 100%, and why does a self-locking jack stay below about 50%?
quiz.a: Work is lost to friction on the thread, so η = tan α/tan(α + φ) < 1. Self-locking needs φ ≥ α, and at φ = α the value is (1 − tan²α)/2 ≈ 0.5, falling as φ grows.

quiz.q: A jack with r = 24 mm, L = 6 mm (single start) and μ = 0.12 raises W = 8 kN. Find the torque and the efficiency.
The torque on a jack screw is 60 N·m. What effort is needed at a handle of radius 400 mm?
quiz.a: P = T/R = 60/0.4 = 150 N. The handle radius, not the screw radius, is used.

quiz.q: Two jacks lift the same load with the same μ but different leads. Jack A has the coarser thread. Compare their torque, efficiency and self-locking safety.
quiz.a: Coarser thread means larger L and larger α. Then tan(α + φ) grows, so torque grows; efficiency tan α/tan(α + φ) rises; and the margin φ − α shrinks, so self-locking is less safe. A very coarse thread may not lock at all.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real lifting screws use square or trapezoidal threads, and recirculating ball screws replace sliding friction with rolling, pushing efficiency past 90% and losing self-locking, so those axes need a brake. The same torque equation sizes the lead screw of a lathe, a CNC table and a hospital bed. Collar and V-thread corrections, thread stresses and buckling of a long screw come later. Search 'power screw efficiency', 'self-locking screw' and 'ball screw backdriving'.
